chunks: Jaʿfar ibn Bashīr narrated from Muʿallā Abī ʿUthmān, from Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said:

I asked him about a man whom an animal approached and wanted to trample, and he feared that from it, so he drove the animal away, and it bolted with its rider and threw him down, resulting in a wound or something else. He said: “There is no liability upon him; he only drove it away from himself, and it is al-jubār.”

key_terms.الْجُبَارُ: Harm deemed uncompensated, with no indemnity due
key_terms.دَابَّةٌ: A riding animal or beast involved in the incident
key_terms.ضَمَانٌ: Legal liability or financial responsibility for damage
key_terms.فَزَجَرَ الدَّابَّةَ: He rebuked or drove the animal away to ward it off

ai.seo_question: Is a person liable if he frightens an animal in self-defense and it injures its rider?
ai.summary: This hadith gives a legal ruling that a person is not liable if he repels an animal to protect himself from harm and the animal then injures its rider. The ruling rests on self-defense and on the principle that the animal’s resulting harm in this case is treated as jubar, carrying no compensation upon that person.

en.bab-ul-qaim-publications: Hadith.5191 - Jafar ibn Bashir narrated from Mualla Abu Uthman from Abu Abdullah Imam Jafar ibn Muhammad Al-Sadiq (as), who said:

I asked Imam (as) about a man who was approached by an animal that was about to trample him, and fearing harm from it, he shouted at the animal, causing it to panic and throw off its rider, resulting in injury or something similar.
Imam (as) said: "There is no liability upon him. He merely repelled the harm from himself, and the animal (dabbah) is considered Al-jubar (i.e., its resulting harm carries no compensation)."
